title: It now seems possible to vaccinate against cancer

vocab.articleQuote: Billions have been spent, yet the field is notorious for its broken promises.
vocab.meaning: Notorious means famous, but only ever for something bad. A notorious intersection is one everybody knows is dangerous, and a notorious cheater is widely known for cheating, which is why you can never be notorious for kindness. Calling the cancer-vaccine field notorious tells you it is not some obscure corner of science nobody noticed. Everyone in medicine knows the field, and what they know it for is decades of announcements that led nowhere.
examples: That corner by the school gate is notorious for fender benders, so a crossing guard stands there every morning.
Our group chat is notorious for going completely silent the night before a project is due.

vocab.articleQuote: First the caveats: delaying re-occurrence might extend overall survival, but it also might not.
vocab.meaning: A caveat is a warning or a condition attached to a claim, the sentence beginning "but keep in mind" that stops you believing more than the evidence supports. It comes from the Latin for "let him beware." Here the writer reports that the vaccine slowed the return of melanoma and then immediately lists three caveats: a delay might not actually lengthen anyone's life, the benefit might be small next to an enormous price, and melanoma might be an unusually easy cancer to attack. Naming your own caveats is a sign of careful thinking rather than of weak evidence.
examples: I'll drive you to practice, with one caveat: if it rains, we leave twenty minutes earlier.
He said the recipe was easy, though the caveat was that the dough had to sit in the fridge overnight.

vocab.articleQuote: The interim results show the vaccine is indeed working, and by implication that the neoantigen idea works, too.
vocab.meaning: Interim means in between and temporary, filling a gap until the real or final version arrives. A school with an interim principal has someone holding the job until a permanent one is hired, and an interim report is a progress update rather than a conclusion. In a drug trial, interim results are what researchers can see partway through, before the study has run its full course. That one word is carrying a lot of weight in this article, because it separates "the vaccine is working so far" from "the vaccine works."
examples: Our teacher posts interim grades in October so we know where we stand well before finals.
Until the school hires a new coach in the spring, an interim coach is running our practices.

concepts.name: Antigens
concepts.articleQuote: The idea of a cancer vaccine is to alert the immune system to mutated proteins, known as neoantigens, found in tumours.
concepts.meaning:
An antigen is a molecule that an immune cell can stick to. That is the whole definition. Immunology is the study of how the body defends itself, and much of it comes down to which molecules stick to which.

Immune cells are white blood cells, and they work by physical contact. Each one carries thousands of copies of a receptor on its outer surface. A receptor is a protein with a particular shape, and it sticks to molecules whose shape fits it, the way a key fits one lock and not the others. Scientists call this binding. Nothing in it involves noticing or choosing. Either two shapes fit and stick together, or they do not and nothing happens.

So what makes a molecule count as foreign? Not the fact that it is harmful. While immune cells are developing, any cell whose receptor sticks strongly to the body's own molecules is destroyed before it is released into the blood. Enormous numbers are destroyed this way. The cells left over are the ones that do not stick to you. After that, foreign means only one thing: a shape that one of the surviving receptors happens to fit.

Two everyday facts show that this is really how it works. Pollen cannot hurt anybody, and it gives people hay fever. A transplanted kidney is keeping its owner alive, and the body destroys it unless that person takes drugs every day to stop that happening. Neither one is dangerous. Both carry shapes that some surviving receptor fits.

There is a second part to this, and the article depends on it. Your cells break down a small share of the proteins they build, and other molecules carry the broken pieces out to the cell surface and hold them there, pointing outward. Almost every cell in your body does this all the time. So the outside of a cell carries samples of the proteins being built inside it, where an immune cell's receptor can reach them.

The article's word follows directly. Neo means new. A neoantigen is one of those pieces on the cell surface that no cell in the body has ever carried before, because the gene that built it was damaged and now produces a slightly different protein. It did not come from outside the body. It is new, and under the rule above that has the same effect.

So when you read that an immune system detects or recognises something, picture shapes fitting together, with nothing in the process making a choice.

concepts.name: T cells
concepts.articleQuote: If the system clocks these as foreign it will eliminate cells that have them.
concepts.meaning:
The article says the immune system will eliminate cells carrying mutated proteins. The cell that does the eliminating is called a T cell, and the article never mentions it.

A T cell is a type of white blood cell. The T stands for thymus, a small organ behind the breastbone where T cells finish developing. You have hundreds of billions of them. Each one carries many thousands of copies of a single receptor shape on its surface, and that receptor sticks to the protein pieces other cells hold on their outer surface.

A T cell moves through blood and tissue, touching other cells briefly as it goes. One of two things happens at each contact. If its receptors stick to the pieces on the other cell's surface, that sticking sets off a series of chemical changes inside the T cell. The T cell then releases proteins that make small holes in the other cell's outer membrane and start the process that makes that cell break itself down. If the receptors do not stick, the contact ends and nothing happens. There is no step in between.

Killing cells on contact is a dangerous thing for a body to allow, and it does go wrong. When T cells destroy healthy tissue the result is an autoimmune disease. In type 1 diabetes, T cells destroy the cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

So there is a second kind of sticking that stops the killing. Many healthy cells carry a particular molecule on their surface that stops the killing, and T cells carry a receptor that this molecule fits. When those two stick together, the chemical changes inside the T cell shut down and it does not kill. That pair of molecules is what the word checkpoint refers to.

This is what the article means when it says tumours suppress an immune response. Cancer cells divide constantly with damaged DNA, so no two are quite alike. A cancer cell that happens to make a lot of that stop molecule is not killed, and it keeps dividing. One that makes little of it is killed, and its copies go with it. After a few months most cells in the tumour make a lot of it. The tumour has not worked anything out and is not doing anything clever. The cells without the molecule were destroyed, so the ones that remain are the ones that had it.

A checkpoint inhibitor is a drug built to stick to one half of that pair before the other half can. While it is in place, the tumour's stop molecule and the T cell's receptor cannot reach each other, the shutdown never starts, and the T cell kills the cell it is touching. The side effects come from the same fact. The stop step is blocked everywhere in the body, not only at the tumour, so T cells sometimes destroy healthy tissue, and patients on these drugs can develop autoimmune problems.

An off switch like the checkpoint is usually not a weakness in a system. It is the reason the system is safe to have at all. When something takes advantage of one, getting rid of it is rarely the answer. This treatment blocks it for a while and accepts the damage that causes.

concepts.name: Antibodies
concepts.articleQuote: using mRNA technology developed for vaccination against infections
concepts.meaning:
Most vaccines work through antibodies. A vaccine against your own cancer cannot, and the reason is a physical limit.

An antibody is a protein, roughly Y-shaped, built and released by a white blood cell called a B cell. A T cell's receptors stay attached to the T cell, but an antibody does not stay attached to the B cell that made it. Your blood carries millions of copies of it, moving freely.

Each antibody has two ends shaped to stick to one particular molecule. When it meets that molecule on the outside of a virus particle or a bacterium, it sticks and stays stuck. Two useful things follow. The antibody is now covering the part of the virus that would have attached to one of your cells, so that virus can no longer get in. And other immune cells have receptors that stick to the far end of an antibody, so a virus covered in antibodies gets swallowed up and broken apart. This is what most vaccines produce. Your body builds antibodies against a molecule found on a virus before you ever meet that virus, so the virus is stuck to and cleared while it is still in the blood.

Now the limit. An antibody is a large protein and it cannot pass through the membrane around a cell. It can only ever stick to something on the outside of a cell. A virus travelling in the blood can be reached. The same virus, once it is inside one of your cells, cannot.

A cancer cell is one of your own cells, and its mutated protein is built inside it. There is nothing floating in the blood for an antibody to stick to. The only place that mutated protein can be reached is the small piece of it the cell holds on its outer surface, and the cells with receptors for those pieces are T cells. That is why a vaccine against a person's own cancer has to produce T cells rather than antibodies.

One last fact connects the two halves. Checkpoint inhibitors, the drugs given alongside this vaccine, are antibodies themselves. They are not made by the patient's B cells, they are manufactured, and the molecule they stick to is not part of a virus but the one on a cell surface that shuts T cells down. Many modern drugs are antibodies chosen this way, to stick to one particular molecule and cover it up.

So the immune system has two parts that reach different places. Antibodies deal with what is outside cells, and T cells deal with what is inside them. When someone says a treatment boosts the immune system, the question worth asking is which part, because help aimed at the wrong one cannot physically reach the problem.

quiz.question: The article says the cancer-vaccine field "is notorious for its broken promises." What is that telling you about the field?
options: It is a small, obscure corner of research that few scientists have bothered with
It is widely known, and what it is known for is repeatedly failing to deliver
Its published results have been shown to be deliberately faked
Regulators have refused to allow research in it
quiz.explanation: Notorious means famous specifically for something bad, so the field is well known in medicine and known for decades of announcements that came to nothing.

quiz.question: The article says the immune system acts if it "clocks these as foreign." What actually makes a molecule count as foreign?
options: It is harmful to the body
Some immune cell has a receptor whose shape sticks to it, because cells whose receptors stick to the body's own molecules are destroyed while they are developing
It originally came from outside the body
It is a protein rather than a fat or a sugar
quiz.explanation: Harmless pollen causes hay fever and a life-saving transplanted kidney gets destroyed, so being harmful is not the test; what matters is whether a surviving receptor fits that shape.

quiz.question: Why is the melanoma vaccine given together with a checkpoint inhibitor rather than on its own?
options: The checkpoint inhibitor stops the vaccine breaking down in the bloodstream
Many cancer cells carry a molecule that sticks to a receptor on the T cell and shuts its killing down, and the inhibitor sticks to one half of that pair first so the two cannot reach each other
The checkpoint inhibitor destroys the tumour while the vaccine prevents infection after surgery
Drug regulators require every cancer trial to test two drugs together
quiz.explanation: A T cell stops killing when that pair of molecules sticks together, so a vaccine that produces T cells achieves nothing until the inhibitor blocks that step.

quiz.question: Why can a vaccine against your own cancer not work the way a flu shot works, by producing antibodies?
options: Antibodies are too small to stick to something as large as a cancer cell
An antibody cannot pass through the membrane around a cell, so it only reaches the outside of cells, and a cancer cell's mutated protein is built inside it
The body stops producing new antibodies in adulthood
Antibodies stick only to bacteria, never to viruses or to human cells
quiz.explanation: Antibodies work on things outside cells, such as a virus in the blood, so reaching a protein built inside one of your own cells is a job for T cells instead.

quiz.question: The article reports interim results and then immediately lists its caveats. Which of these is NOT one of the caveats it raises?
options: Delaying the return of the cancer might not actually mean patients live longer
The benefit could turn out to be small while the treatment is enormously expensive
Melanoma provokes the immune system unusually strongly, so other cancers may respond less well
Personalised vaccines cannot be manufactured quickly enough for individual patients
quiz.explanation: A caveat is a warning attached to a claim, and the article raises the first three; manufacturing speed is the problem mRNA technology already solved, not a remaining doubt.
